claims.text: In Pt/Cu single-atom alloys, isolated Pt atoms are embedded in a Cu matrix.
Isolated Pt atoms in a Cu matrix modify the electronic structure of the active sites.
The modified electronic structure tunes adsorption energies of propane-dehydrogenation intermediates.
The tuned adsorption energies favor propylene desorption over excessive dehydrogenation.
Favoring propylene desorption increases propane-dehydrogenation selectivity and conversion relative to conventional Pt-based alloys.
Optimized support interactions or protective coatings can keep Pt atoms individually dispersed under high-temperature reaction conditions.
Isolation of individual Pt atoms within the Cu matrix creates active sites with adsorption characteristics distinct from conventional Pt-alloy sites.
Isolated Pt sites alter conventional adsorption-energy scaling relationships.
Altered scaling relationships reduce the binding energy of dehydrogenated species.
Reduced binding of dehydrogenated species promotes selective propylene desorption.
Reduced binding of dehydrogenated species minimizes over-dehydrogenation and side reactions.
At about 520 °C and atmospheric pressure, the Pt/Cu single-atom alloy is predicted to have higher propylene selectivity than the conventional Pt-alloy baseline.
The targeted propylene selectivity is approximately 90%.
The Pt/Cu single-atom alloy is predicted to provide higher overall propane conversion than the conventional Pt-alloy baseline.
The proposed behavior is conditional on maintaining single-atom Pt dispersion while controlling particle size and support material.
Long-term high-temperature operation may destabilize isolated Pt atoms through sintering.
Minor Pt sintering may affect catalytic performance.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant selectivity and conversion improvement while sustained single-atom dispersion is verified would falsify the hypothesis.
